source_text:
Ἐγὼ γράφω πάσαις ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις, καὶ ἐντέλλομαι πᾶσιν, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἑκὼν ὑπὲρ θεοῦ ἀποθνήσκω, ἐάνπερ ὑμεῖς μὴ κωλύσητε. παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς, μὴ εὔνοια ἄκαιρος γένησθέ μοι. ἄφετέ με θηρίων εἶναι βοράν, δἰ ὦν ἔνεστιν θεοῦ ἐπιτυχεῖν. σῖτός εἰμι θεοῦ καὶ δἰ ὀδόντων θηρίων ἀλήθομαι, ἵνα καθαρὸς ἄρτος εὑρεθῶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ.
μᾶλλον κολακεύσατε τὰ θηρία, ἵνα μοι τάφος γένωνται καὶ μηθὲν καταλίπωσι τῶν τοῦ σώματός μου, ἵνα μὴ κοιμηθεὶς βαρύς τινι γένωμαι. τότε ἔσομαι μαθητὴς ἀληθῶς Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὅτε οὐδὲ τὸ σῶμά μου ὁ κόσμος ὄψεται. λιτανεύσατε τὸν Χριστὸν ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ, ἵνα διὰ τῶν ὀργάνων τούτων θυσία εὑρεθῶ.
οὐχ ὡς Πέτρος καὶ Παῦλος διατάσσομαι ὑμῖν. ἐκεῖνοι ἀπόστολοι, ἐγὼ κατάκριτος: ἐκεῖνοι ἐλεύθεροι, ἐγὼ δὲ μέχρι νῦν δοῦλος. ἀλλ’ ἐὰν πάθω, ἀπελεύθερος γενήσομαι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἀναστήσομαι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐλεύθερος. νῦν μανθάνω δεδεμένος μηδὲν ἐπιθυμεῖν.
thought_title: Wheat ground by beasts into pure bread
orientation: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writes to the church in Rome while being taken under guard to martyrdom, and here he begs them not to prevent his death by wild beasts.
pass_a_gloss: I write to all the churches, and I command all, that I willingly for God am dying, if only you do not prevent [me]. I beg you, do not [become] an untimely kindness to me. Allow me to be food of beasts, through whom it is possible to attain God. Wheat of God I am, and through teeth of beasts I am ground, so that pure bread of Christ I may be found. Rather coax the beasts, so that a tomb for me they may become and nothing they may leave behind of the [parts] of my body, so that not having fallen asleep heavy to anyone I may become. Then I will be a disciple truly of Jesus Christ, when not even my body the world will see. Beseech Christ for me, so that through these instruments a sacrifice I may be found. Not as Peter and Paul I command you. Those [men are] apostles, I [am] a condemned man; those [men are] free, I but until now [am] a slave. But if I suffer, a freedman I will become of Jesus Christ and I will rise in him free. Now I am learning, bound, nothing to desire.

choices.why: Keeps the present tense of ἀποθνήσκω, which expresses Ignatius's present resolve as he writes, not a future event
rejected: I am willing to die for God

choices.english: do not become an untimely kindness to me
choices.why: Preserves the noun εὔνοια with the adjective ἄκαιρος, keeping the idea that even well-meaning kindness can be wrong if it prevents martyrdom
rejected: do not show me untimely favor
do not be kind to me at the wrong time

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of wheat, which is central to the image of being ground by teeth into bread
rejected: I am the grain of God

choices.why: The passive voice shows the beasts are the agents of grinding, matching the source
The verb means to coax or entice, and Ignatius uses it ironically to urge the Romans to encourage the beasts to devour him
The term specifically means a freed slave, which fits Ignatius's contrast between his present slavery and future freedom in Christ

pass_b_english: I am writing to all the churches and declaring to everyone that I die willingly for God, unless you prevent me. I beg you: do not show me a kindness that comes at the wrong time. Let me be food for the beasts, for through them I can attain God. I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ.

Coax the beasts instead, so that they may become my tomb and leave nothing of my body behind, so that when I have fallen asleep I may burden no one. Then I will truly be a disciple of Jesus Christ, when the world no longer sees even my body. Pray to Christ for me, so that through these instruments I may be found a sacrifice.

I do not give you orders as Peter and Paul did. They were apostles; I am a condemned man. They were free; I am still a slave. But if I suffer, I will become a freedman of Jesus Christ and will rise in him free. Now, bound as I am, I am learning to desire nothing.

last_rejected.quote: I am learning to desire nothing
last_rejected.why: Ignatius learns not to desire, not 'learning to desire nothing' which suggests active pursuit of emptiness.
last_rejected.fix: Now, bound as I am, I am learning to want nothing.
last_rejected.ruling: μανθάνω + infinitive means 'learning to [infinitive]'; 'learning to desire nothing' correctly renders μηδὲν ἐπιθυμεῖν.

problems.quote: I beg you: do not become an untimely kindness to me
problems.why: 'Untimely kindness' is paradoxical; means 'ill-timed act of mercy' (preventing martyrdom).
problems.fix: Revise to 'do not show me ill-timed mercy'.

problems.quote: I do not command you as Peter and Paul do
problems.why: Not a scripture citation but historical claim; no issue unless reader expects biblical reference.
Different animal metaphors for false teachers may blur into literal beasts of martyrdom.
problems.fix: Clarify which are metaphorical vs. literal where ambiguity arises.

edits.old: do not become an untimely kindness to me
edits.new: do not show me ill-timed mercy

fixed: The 'untimely kindness' phrase was a real mistranslation and has been revised to 'ill-timed mercy'.
The 'Peter and Paul' statement is a historical claim, not a scripture citation; no fix needed.
The 'rabid dogs' issue does not appear in the provided English text; no fix needed.

problems.why: 'Flatter' seems absurd—how does one flatter animals? Greek kolakeuo may mean 'coax' or 'fawn upon,' but the image is still strange.
problems.fix: Add note: rhetorical paradox; Ignatius means 'encourage' or 'incite' the beasts to do their worst.

fixed: Changed 'flatter' to 'coax' to better capture the sense of kolakeuo as inciting or encouraging the beasts, avoiding the absurdity of flattering animals.

polish.changed: Clarified that Ignatius is declaring rather than commanding, softened the comparison to Peter and Paul to avoid implying they merely commanded, and made the pronoun references and sentence flow more natural for modern readers while preserving every claim.

notes.why: 'Mad dogs' and 'wild beasts' both describe false teachers, but 'beasts' also describes martyrdom animals; reader may conflate.
notes.fix: Clarify 'mad dogs' is metaphor for heretics, 'beasts' for martyrdom.

notes.quote: I do not command you as Peter and Paul do
notes.why: Ignatius claims lesser authority, but 'command' seems strong for apostles too; may mean 'with apostolic authority.'
notes.fix: Note: Ignatius acknowledges Petrine and Pauline authority in Roman church.

notes.why: 'Ten leopards' is a metaphor for soldiers, but 'beasts' later in the same letter means actual animals for execution.
notes.fix: Add a note: 'ten leopards—that is, a detachment of soldiers' (already present) and distinguish from literal beasts.
